stemMd: A student hypothesised that **Variety S is better suited than Variety R to soils that hold little water.** Do the results of Study 1 support this hypothesis?

options.label: A
options.textMd: No; as soil water content rose from 10% to 40%, the mean root length of Variety S decreased steadily.

options.label: B
options.textMd: Yes; at 10% and 20% soil water, Variety S had both higher germination and longer roots than Variety R.

options.label: C
options.textMd: No; at both 30% and 40% soil water, Variety S had lower germination and shorter roots than Variety R did.

options.label: D
options.textMd: Yes; Variety S's maximum germination, reached at 20% soil water, was higher than Variety R's maximum.

explanationMd:
First decide which rows of Table 1 the hypothesis is actually about. "Soils that hold little water" means the **low** water contents, so the relevant rows are 10% and 20% — not the whole table.

Now compare the two varieties in exactly those rows:

| Water content | R germination | S germination | R root | S root |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10% | 18% | 42% | 9 mm | 21 mm |
| 20% | 56% | 78% | 24 mm | 38 mm |

In both low-water rows, Variety S germinates more **and** grows longer roots. Both measured outcomes point the same way, so the data support the hypothesis, and the choice reporting that at 10% and 20% soil water Variety S had both higher germination and longer roots than Variety R states the evidence correctly.

Check your reasoning by asking what evidence *would* have refuted the hypothesis: S doing worse than R at 10% or 20% water. That does not happen. What S does at 30% and 40% water is real, but it is evidence about wet soil, and the hypothesis makes no claim about wet soil at all — which is exactly why the choice citing S's lower germination and shorter roots at 30% and 40% water, though its figures are true, does not refute anything.

distractorRationale.d: Reaches the right verdict from a false figure. Variety S's maximum germination was indeed reached at 20% water, but it was 78%, while Variety R reached 88% at 30% water, so S's maximum was not the higher one; $78 < 88$.
distractorRationale.c: Cites figures that are true — at 30% water S germinated 74% to R's 88% with 33 mm roots to R's 41 mm, and at 40% water 40% to 62% with 16 mm to 30 mm — but uses them to answer a question about *dry* soils. Performance in wet soil is outside the scope of a hypothesis about soils that hold little water, so it cannot refute it.
distractorRationale.a: Misreads the Variety S root-length column. From 10% to 40% water those values are 21, 38, 33 and 16 mm: they rise before they fall, so root length does not decrease steadily, and the stated reason is simply not what the table shows.

accessibilityText: The question asks whether the results of Study 1, given in Table 1 of the germination passage, support the hypothesis that Variety S is better suited than Variety R to soils that hold little water. Table 1 is read out in full with the passage. The four choices, in order, are: no, because Variety S root length fell steadily as soil water rose from 10 to 40 percent; yes, because at 10 and 20 percent soil water Variety S had both higher germination and longer roots than Variety R; no, because at 30 and 40 percent soil water Variety S had lower germination and shorter roots than Variety R; yes, because Variety S's maximum germination, at 20 percent soil water, was higher than Variety R's maximum.

independentSolve.workingNotes: At 10% water S germinated 42% vs R 18% with roots 21 vs 9 mm; at 20% S had 78% vs 56% and 38 vs 24 mm, so S outperforms R in low-water soil and the hypothesis is supported. S's roots go 21, 38, 33, 16, not a steady decrease; the high-water comparison is accurate but irrelevant to low-water suitability; S's maximum (78%) is below R's (88%). [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-cue-batch1-run1) reached the same answer: At low water S beats R on both measures. At 10%: germination 42 vs 18, roots 21 vs 9. At 20%: germination 78 vs 56, roots 38 vs 24. So the data support the hypothesis. The 'S roots decreased steadily' option is false (21, 38, 33, 16). The 'S maximum higher' option is false (78 vs 88). The 'No; at 30% and 40% S was lower' option states true facts, but they concern wet soil and do not bear on a hypothesis about dry soil.]

review.notes: Author solved the item and attempted to defend each distractor before keying it. Scope is the load-bearing point: the hypothesis concerns low water contents only, so the 10% and 20% rows decide it and both favour Variety S on both measures. The 'no' option quoting the 30% and 40% rows states true figures but answers a different question, and the other two options misstate the maximum germination and the root-length trend. Awaiting an independent blind solve.
